dialogue_inspector.speaker: Inspector
lines: Welcome to New Jalpaiguri, Tenzing. From this platform the plains end and the Himalayas begin.
Your blue toy train runs on a narrow two-foot gauge — one of the smallest working railways in the world.

dialogue_boatman.speaker: Boatman
lines: Sumendu Lake is the heart of Mirik. Pine forests on one shore, an orange orchard road on the other.
The wooden Indreni footbridge crosses the water at its narrowest point — the locals call it the rainbow bridge.
Row gently here, Tenzing. The lake is fed by springs from the surrounding ridges, and the surface remembers every ripple.

dialogue_old_traveler.speaker: Old Traveler
lines: Rohini Road is the newest route to the hills — opened in the 2000s after the old Pankhabari road grew too steep for buses.
Watch the prayer flags strung between the pines. The five colours stand for sky, air, fire, water, and earth.
If the mist closes in, slow down and listen. On these bends the mountain tells you what the eyes cannot see.

dialogue_tea_worker.speaker: Tea Worker
lines: We pluck only two leaves and a bud — that is the rule for true Darjeeling tea.
The first flush of spring is the most prized harvest in the world; some call it the champagne of teas.

dialogue_darjeeling_tea_worker.speaker: Tea Worker
lines: Darjeeling town sits at about 2,000 metres above the sea. The air is thinner here, and so are the clouds.
From Tiger Hill at dawn, the Kanchenjunga turns gold before the sun has even reached our rooftops.
Mall Road and Chowrasta have been the meeting place of this town since the British days — but the chai stalls belong to us.

dialogue_monk.speaker: Monk
lines: Welcome to Ghoom, Tenzing. At 2,258 metres, you stand at the highest railway station in India.
Inside our gompa, the Maitreya Buddha rises fifteen feet tall — the future Buddha, waiting in patience for his age to come.
Spin the prayer wheels clockwise as you pass. Each turn releases a mantra into the wind, carried out across the hills.
Even the heaviest fog lifts in time. The mountains teach us that nothing — joy or sorrow — stays forever.

dialogue_monk_stage5.speaker: Monk
lines: Yiga Choeling — our old name. Founded in 1850 by the Mongolian monk Sokpo Sherab Gyatso, the oldest Tibetan monastery in the Darjeeling hills.
The Maitreya you see was built from clay brought all the way from Tibet, mixed with the waters of these hills.
Books in our library are written in Tibetan, on long paper leaves wrapped in silk. Some are over a hundred years old.

dialogue_guide_trail.speaker: Guide
lines: The Singalila ridge is the spine we follow. To your left lies Nepal, to your right is India — the trail walks the border.
In spring these slopes turn red and pink with rhododendron — Sikkim's state flower, and the soul of these forests.
Sandakphu rises to 3,636 metres. From there you can see four of the world's five tallest peaks in a single horizon.

dialogue_guide_trail_old.speaker: Guide
lines: Take small breaths and small steps. Above 3,000 metres the body learns a different rhythm.
Tonglu, Tumling, Kalipokhri — each shelter on the way has its own story and its own stove.

dialogue_guide_summit.speaker: Guide
lines: You stand on Sandakphu now — the highest point in West Bengal.
From here, the clouds drift below us instead of above.

lines.speaker: Wise Traveler
lines.text: Wait for the first light, Tenzing. As the sun rises, Kanchenjunga takes the shape of a Sleeping Buddha lying across the sky.

lines.speaker: Wise Traveler
lines.text: The head is the peak of Kabru, the body is Kanchenjunga itself, and the feet stretch toward Pandim.

lines.speaker: Wise Traveler
lines.text: Everest, Lhotse, Makalu, Kanchenjunga — four of the world's five highest peaks, all visible from this single ridge.

lines.speaker: Wise Traveler
lines.text: You have come a long way from the platforms of NJP. The mountains remember every traveler who reaches them.

lines.speaker: Mountain Guide
lines.text: On the clearest mornings, the snow line of Kanchenjunga catches fire — first orange, then gold, then white.

lines.speaker: Mountain Guide
lines.text: Travelers wait silently for this moment. The mountains do not perform; they simply appear, and we are lucky to witness them.

DIALOG_STAGE_7_SUMMIT.speaker: Wise Traveler
lines: There — see how Kanchenjunga lies on her side? That is the Sleeping Buddha the old maps speak of.
Kanchenjunga rises to 8,586 metres, the third highest mountain on earth, and the guardian of Sikkim.
The toy train carried you out of the plains; the Rohini road carried you up the hills; but only your own feet brought you here.
Every prayer wheel you turned at Ghoom, every cup of tea in Darjeeling, every bend of the Singalila ridge — all of it is part of this view.
Rest now, Tenzing. The mountains were here long before you, and they will remain. But for this morning, you are part of them.

lines.speaker: Monk
lines.text: Welcome to Yiga Choeling — Ghoom Monastery. The wheels you hear turning are filled with mantras, one for every revolution.

lines.speaker: Monk
lines.text: Travelers have stopped here for more than 170 years. Some come for the Buddha, some for the silence, some only for shelter from the fog.

lines.speaker: Tea Worker
lines.text: Darjeeling has 87 tea gardens — Happy Valley, just below the town, is the oldest still working.

lines.speaker: Tea Worker
lines.text: Our tea bushes were grown from seeds the British carried out of China in the 1800s. They took to these hills as if they had always belonged here.

lines.speaker: Tea Worker
lines.text: Darjeeling tea was the first Indian product to receive the GI tag — only tea grown in these hills can be sold under that name.

lines.speaker: Tea Worker
lines.text: Cool mist, sloping soil, and high altitude give our leaves their muscatel flavour — a taste no other garden in the world can copy.
